We said that poetry became quieter during this period while public speaking took the leading role.

The first was objective. Poetry belongs to the process of artistic creation, and artistic creation does not easily or quickly adapt itself to a major new change. To produce art that feels genuine, the artist needs inner conviction and deep emotional involvement.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This inner emotional truth is an essential part of creating great art. But an artist cannot simply manufacture or force it. If it is manufactured, it is no longer genuine.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

This is why literature and art often respond to major social and historical changes only after some delay. Their own role in the two-way interaction between culture and society’s underlying structures is therefore delayed as well.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This was the position of Arabic poetry when Islam first appeared.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Poetry did not respond easily or quickly to this great new development in Arab society. In fact, at first the opposite happened. A number of poets from Quraysh rose to defend the Qurayshi leadership against the Islamic movement.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The second main reason for the decline of poetry came from Islam’s own attitude toward it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Islam brought the Qur’an with a highly developed artistic style. Its aesthetic qualities had reached a very high level and matched the development of the Arabs’ own literary and rhetorical taste during the pre-Islamic period.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Islam wanted this striking new artistic event to become the main attraction for people’s emotions and literary tastes, so that the Qur’an’s rhetorical and aesthetic appeal would itself become a path toward religious faith.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
For this purpose, Islam did not rely only on the Qur’an’s own artistic power. Nor did it rely only on presenting the Qur’an as a miraculous divine phenomenon beyond human ability.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
In addition to all this, the Qur’an itself launched an attack on poetry and poets.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
At first, this helped spread an attitude of hostility toward poetry and poets among those responding to the Qur’anic attack.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But poetry and poets had such a strong influence over the people of pre-Islamic society that it was not easy to abolish their role or turn people away from them completely.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
That was a difficult and unrealistic goal.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Poets who supported the old tribal leadership continued their counter-campaign. Eventually the Prophet and his companions had to fight poetry with poetry.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
They turned to Ḥassān ibn Thābit, one of the prominent poets of the pre-Islamic period who had since become a Muslim, and asked him to answer the attacks.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
He began writing poems in praise of the Prophet and satirical poems against his enemies. This is how Ḥassān became known as “the Prophet’s poet.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam

But if we compare Ḥassān’s poetry from this period with the poetry he had written before Islam, there is a noticeable difference in artistic quality. His earlier poetry was more creative and showed greater artistic sincerity.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
All this took place during the early years of the Islamic movement.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Later, as people became increasingly occupied with the new religion and Islam spread more widely across Arabia, this poetic battle died down. The energy of poetry itself declined with it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Poetry began to regain its force only when conflict returned to society in new forms, beginning with the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and continuing afterward.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

While poetry was relatively quiet, public speaking carried out the work of “propaganda and agitation.” Both its style and its content drew heavily on the Qur’an and on its religious, legal, and moral themes.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

This gave public speaking the chance to develop greatly and continuously until the Abbasid period. By then, prose writing and the production of scientific and philosophical works had begun to overshadow it. Poetry too regained a major role, shaped by the intellectual, social, and cultural development that had taken place.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
All these cultural forms, as well as the Islamic texts themselves, were transmitted mainly by word of mouth.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Writing had not been widely used in pre-Islamic society, and even during the first Islamic period its spread remained fairly limited.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Writing in Arabia did, however, have a long history.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The historical evidence known so far does not reveal written remains from the ancient Arab peoples before the kingdom of Saba in southern Arabia. Saba came after the Minaean kingdom and had its own writing system, which is described as the earliest old form of present-day Arabic writing.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Its ancient name was “cuneiform writing,” and its letters were known as the Musnad script. Archaeologists have found examples of this writing in Sabaean inscriptions on stone and metal, and especially on copper tablets.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The point is that writing in the Arabian Peninsula was ancient. It must have passed through several stages of development before reaching the form of Arabic writing known in the late pre-Islamic and early Islamic periods.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It cannot simply have appeared suddenly in those periods already in the relatively developed form it had then.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The difference between the Arabic writing we use today and the writing of the first Islamic period, judging from the handwritten documents that have survived from that time, is not extremely large.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This suggests that writing in the Islamic period must already have had a much longer history before reaching the form we find in those documents.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
In general, then, writing was rare in Arabia at the time, but it did exist.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

When the Prophet and his companions migrated to Medina, seventeen Muslim men and three Muslim women knew how to write. Among them were people later known as “the scribes of revelation,” including Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, and Zayd ibn Thābit.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The needs of the new Islamic community made it necessary to spread writing more widely among Muslims.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
They began looking for people who already knew how to write so that they could teach others.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

After the Muslim victory over Quraysh at the Battle of Badr, a number of prisoners were taken. Muhammad then issued a rule that any prisoner who taught ten people in Medina to write would be released.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This differed from pre-Islamic custom, under which money had been the only ransom for release from captivity.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Writing therefore began to spread, and with it came a certain amount of religious education.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
There is also a report that the Prophet once encouraged some of his companions to learn another language in addition to Arabic.

We have seen that Islam appeared in the Arabian Peninsula at the beginning of the seventh century, at a time when pre-Islamic society was going through major social changes affecting the very foundations on which that society was built.

We also saw that the rise of Islam at this stage of Arab history did not take place separately from the events that were shaking the foundations of the old tribal social order and its particular historical features.

We therefore looked for the relationship between these events—which pointed toward some kind of change in the lives of the people of Arabia—and the great new development announced by Muhammad as a divine religion revealed to him by God.

We began to find the first thread leading us toward this relationship when we examined the connection, before the rise of Islam, between Muhammad himself and the religious and intellectual current that had first appeared in one of Arabia’s agricultural regions and then spread into other settled and semi-settled areas.
We mean the movement known in pre-Islamic Arab history, and in Islamic history itself, as the religion of the Hanifs.
It was not by chance that Islam was described in both the Qur’an and the Prophet’s hadiths as the Hanif religion.

Historians tell us that Muhammad was either one of these Hanifs or was closely connected with them. We saw this as further evidence that, when Islam appeared in Arabia, it was an objective continuation, at a new stage of development, of the Hanif movement itself.
That movement had emerged during a period when social relations in the desert, the cities, and the agricultural regions were gradually beginning to undergo new changes.

We also found that the Hanif movement reflected changes taking place in the intellectual ideas and spiritual outlook of pre-Islamic society. These changes were themselves connected to the early transformation of the tribal system and its old, relatively primitive character.
From this, we identified several important social and intellectual roots on which Islam was built when it appeared under those particular historical conditions.
To identify these roots more precisely, we first examined the social background from which Muhammad emerged.
Second, we looked at the class structure of the population of Mecca, where Islam first appeared.
Third, we examined the general foundations and principles on which Islam built both its religious beliefs and its laws.
This led us to the following conclusions:

1 — Islam, in its essential and practical content—and even in its religious form and its metaphysical and idealist concepts—was an objective response to the historical changes needed by pre-Islamic society.
Sometimes this response was direct, and sometimes it was less visible.
It was also a response to the sharp contradictions found in some places, such as Mecca, and the milder contradictions found elsewhere, such as among unsettled Bedouin communities.
Although these contradictions appeared in different social, spiritual, and intellectual forms, almost all of them could be traced back to the same material base.
That material base lay in the gradual breakdown of the tribal system.

The old natural, largely self-sufficient economy was weakening. Trade, money, and interest-based lending were spreading. At the same time, differences between rich and poor were becoming more visible.
On one side stood the great merchants, moneylenders, and tribal chiefs.
On the other stood small traders, craftspeople, wage workers, the destitute, people crushed by heavy interest-bearing debts, and ordinary members of the tribes.
2 — The two central principles on which Islamic belief was mainly built—monotheism and resurrection—also had social roots beneath their religious meaning.
In religious terms, monotheism means belief in one God who created the universe, and then in one religion.
But behind this idea of unity we can also see what may have been an indirect reflection of the idea of social unity.
Pre-Islamic tribal society was fragmented. The historical need was to bring its separate tribal units together on a new basis, even if that basis was religious.
What mattered was that the breakdown and fragmentation affecting the tribal system at the time required the different tribal groups to be brought together within the framework of one religion.
In social terms, that meant bringing them within the framework of one people.
The principle of resurrection, in its religious meaning, says that another world exists beyond our material world.

But it also carries an almost direct promise to the socially deprived and oppressed: in that other world, they will find compensation for the deprivation and injustice they suffer here, and comfort for the harsh reality of their lives.
At the same time, it threatens their oppressors with punishment in the afterlife.
Yet the forces responsible for social oppression could also benefit from a belief that justice would be postponed until the next world.
3 — Islam did not stop at principles of belief. It also introduced a system of law in which the social effects were much clearer than they were in the religious doctrines themselves.
Islamic law prohibited usury, monopoly, and the hoarding of gold and silver.
It imposed the zakāt tax on certain forms of wealth belonging to the rich and made its proceeds the right of particular groups among the poorest and most needy.
It also introduced rules regulating certain productive and social relationships.
Yet the basic principle of Islamic law still accepted social differentiation.
Even so, these laws came as a shock to the wealthy people of Mecca and spread alarm among them.

They looked at what an Islamic victory might do to their immediate interests. They did not yet have enough class awareness to see that, over the longer term, the general direction of development would not conflict with the development of their own class position.
For this reason, Islam, Muhammad, and the first Muslims faced violent persecution from the wealthy Qurayshi leadership in Mecca.
At the beginning of the Islamic movement, however, Islam did not win many supporters among the poor of Mecca either.
The social laws we have described did not appear until after the migration from Mecca to Medina.
For these poor people, the promise of reward and the threat of punishment on the Day of Resurrection were not enough reason to endure persecution in defence of Islam.
They needed an immediate material answer to their material problems.
4 — Islam also introduced ideas about the metaphysical nature of the universe and the world, about the place of human beings within the universe, and about human responsibility for their actions.

Yet the Qur’an appears contradictory when it comes to defining this responsibility. At some points it presents human beings as free in their actions, while at others it speaks in terms of compulsion and predestination.

5 — In Chapter Two, we also examined the Muslim migration from Mecca to Medina, or Yathrib, along with its causes, its decisive consequences, and the conflict between Mecca and Medina that followed it.

Throughout this conflict, the basic issue remained the same: the changes that the Islamic movement was bringing to the social forms that had dominated pre-Islamic society, especially the society of Mecca.
6 — We then examined the legislative stage of Islam, which began immediately after the migration to Medina.
We saw that the laws introduced during this stage were grounded, for the most part, in material conditions and were closely connected to the practical needs created by the migration itself.
Later, they were also shaped by the victories that the Anṣār and Muhājirūn began to win against the Qurayshi leadership in Mecca.
Eventually that leadership accepted the new reality.
Mecca came under Islam and returned to its position as a religious centre, but now in a new form and under the banner of Islam.
While discussing Islamic law in this chapter, we also pointed to an important feature of its development: the existence of a principle allowing law to change and develop.
